events.credibility_reason: A 4-5 page single-author preprint posted seven days ago claims to settle a question listed as open since 2000. Remark 3.3 extends the result to ω₁-strongly compact cardinals, a much stronger claim that the record could not check. The proof was read only through summaries. No error has been identified, and seven days is too short to expect uptake, so this is not not_credible.

why: You (2026) states Theorem A as exactly the statement: strongly compact κ with GCH below κ implies GCH. So it is scope whole. It has no named reader and was posted a week ago, so it is unreviewed. I marked it doubtful, not not_credible: it is very short, the proof was seen only through summaries, and Remark 3.3's extension to ω₁-strongly compact cardinals is suspiciously strong, but no error is identified and a week is too short to expect any uptake. AI role was the close call. The only evidence is an acknowledgement that the work 'used AI assistance' with the models 'invoked dynamically during the investigation'. It does not say the models produced any argument, construction or case in the result. Under the rule that a thin quote with no stated contribution is none, I answered none. The Goldberg results assume the Ultrapower Axiom (and in one case supercompactness), and Apter (2012) works without full choice, so all are variants. Apter (2000) was never read and Banerjee (2019) is about a different subject, so both are none.
doubts: The AI role for You (2026) could reasonably be read as assisted: 'invoked dynamically during the investigation' implies the models took part in the research, but the paper never says what they produced. If the author later discloses that a model supplied a step, this should change to assisted or generated. The paper's text, including the acknowledgement, was read only through fetch-tool summaries and not checked against the PDF. Remark 3.3 should be checked by an expert, since a false strong extension would cast doubt on the main argument.
